\section[a trovoada]{a trovoada — the thunderstorm}

\label{lesson:PT-C463-trovoada}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for sunstroke, then the Portuguese for to sweat.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a trovoada}
\textbf{a trovoada} — \textquotedblleft{}the thunderstorm\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ontem à noite houve uma trovoada forte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Last night there was a heavy thunderstorm.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{o trovão}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{trovoada} is built on \emph{trovão} 'thunder'. \emph{Trovão} is usually traced to Latin \emph{tonitrus} 'thunder' (Lewis \& Short), with its sounds rearranged, but the details are not settled; EtymDB lists Galician \emph{trebón} as a cousin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a trovoada}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a trovoada}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a trovoada}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for sunstroke, then the Portuguese for to sweat, then say \emph{a trovoada} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a trovoada mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The thunderstorm\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[trovejar]{trovejar — to thunder}

\label{lesson:PT-C463-trovejar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to sweat, then the Portuguese for the thunderstorm.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: trovejar}
\textbf{trovejar} — \textquotedblleft{}to thunder\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Começou a trovejar quando saímos de casa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It started to thunder when we left home.}
\end{quote}

Like \emph{chover}, used without a subject: \emph{troveja}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{trovejar} is built on \emph{trovão} 'thunder', which is usually traced to Latin \emph{tonitrus} 'thunder' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[relampejar]{relampejar — to flash with lightning}

\label{lesson:PT-C463-relampejar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the thunderstorm, then the Portuguese for to thunder.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: relampejar}
\textbf{relampejar} — \textquotedblleft{}to flash with lightning\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Relampeja muito longe, no mar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is lightning far away, over the sea.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{o relâmpago}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{relampejar} is built on \emph{relâmpago} 'lightning', which goes back to Latin \emph{lampas} 'torch, light' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o granizo]{o granizo — hail}

\label{lesson:PT-C463-granizo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to thunder, then the Portuguese for to flash with lightning.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o granizo}
\textbf{o granizo} — \textquotedblleft{}hail\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O granizo partiu o vidro da estufa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The hail broke the greenhouse glass.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Cair granizo} — to hail.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{granizo} was borrowed from Spanish \emph{granizo} (EtymDB), built on \emph{grano} 'grain', from Latin \emph{grānum}: hail falls like grains.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o granizo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o granizo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to thunder, then the Portuguese for to flash with lightning, then say \emph{o granizo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[o aguaceiro]{o aguaceiro — the downpour, the heavy shower}

\label{lesson:PT-C463-aguaceiro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to flash with lightning, then the Portuguese for hail.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o aguaceiro}
\textbf{o aguaceiro} — \textquotedblleft{}the downpour, the heavy shower\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ao meio-dia caiu um aguaceiro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{At midday there was a downpour.}
\end{quote}

Weather forecasts say \emph{aguaceiros} for showers.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aguaceiro} is built on \emph{aguaça} 'lots of water' with \emph{-eiro} (EtymDB); \emph{água} is inherited from Latin \emph{aqua}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to flash with lightning, then the Portuguese for hail, then say \emph{o aguaceiro} again
